description: One plugin for the full lifecycle of a multi-agent Thor team. Deploy a whole team from a blueprint (profiles, SOULs, crons, shared kanban/mesh) with `thor teams deploy`, verify it with Deploy Guard (preflight/smoke/rollback), watch fleet status and the mesh map, catch silent cron gaps (Cron911) and dead models (Model Guard), get a daily standup digest, and broadcast decisions across teams (mesh sync). The Agent Factory is an in-plugin template generator: from a one-line spec it extends a base blueprint with a new role or scaffolds a new team, then deploys it via the same verified pipeline (fixture fallback for demos). 16 tools plus the thor teams CLI. Local-first by default: everything runs against your own THOR_HOME; optional `--host` ssh deploys use your own credentials, nothing is stored; `--host` copies the bundle only to your own host. Disclosure — deploying a team creates Thor profiles and cron jobs in your THOR_HOME; rollback deletes only teamops-prefixed profiles and files under <home>/teams/<team>/; Model Guard apply and rollback rewrite every profile's config.yaml and jobs.json; fleet and cron scans read every profile's cron store; the optional `--host` deploy copies the team bundle to your VPS over your own ssh credentials and trusts a first-seen host key; `thor teams dashboard` runs a token-protected server on 127.0.0.1:8781; the bundled trading blueprint is paper-only by instruction, and its agents get the terminal toolset.

name: thor-telegram-business
description: Observe-with-approval Telegram Business Mode (secretary bot): Thor drafts replies to your customers' messages and DMs each draft to you with Send, Edit and Discard buttons; nothing reaches a customer until you tap Send. A Thor Labs plugin: built by Thor Labs, not supported. Disclosure — each customer message is sent to your active Thor model to draft the reply, and drafts and connection records are stored locally in <THOR_HOME>/telegram-business/state.db.

name: thor-telemetry
description: Observability + budget guardrails for Thor Agent — tokens, cost, latency, tool calls per session and cron job. Persists to local SQLite. Exposes /stats and /budget slash commands. Disclosure — records per-session tokens, cost, latency, tool names and sender/profile ids (no message text; failed API calls keep the provider's error message, truncated to 500 chars) in ~/.thor/telemetry/telemetry.db; fetches public model pricing from openrouter.ai/api/v1/models on first load and at most once a day; in the default enforce mode first load writes a $5/day, $100/month global budget to telemetry/budget.yaml, and a hard breach blocks every tool call and pauses the over-budget cron job until the window resets (set plugins.entries.thor-telemetry.settings.mode: observe to record without enforcing); the optional standalone dashboard server binds 127.0.0.1 with no auth.

name: thor-telemetry-dashboard
description: Dashboard-only read plugin: visualize the shared-metrics telemetry Thor collects locally — metric families, drilldowns, milestone timeline, install snapshot, and the exact next package payload. Send stays off.

name: thor-teleoperator
description: Keep one conversation on the gateway while switching shell, files, skills and explicitly permitted MCP tools between machines over SSH. The standalone Rust receiver needs no Thor or language runtime. Commands have the destination SSH user's full OS authority; this is not a sandbox. Disclosure — Routes this conversation's terminal, file, process, skill and allowlisted MCP tool calls to SSH machines you configure, where the author's Rust receiver runs them with that SSH user's full authority; Thor' dangerous-command and human-approval prompts run before each routed call, but other plugins' pre_tool_call blocks and the agent's tool guardrails do not see routed calls until core adds a seam (thor-agent#152963). The optional `python -m thor_teleoperator.deploy` helper downloads the receiver from the author's GitHub release (SHA256 pinned in the plugin source, build-attested) and installs it on the remote host over SSH; file transfers need approval, and gateway-local transfers stay inside a configured transfer_dir.

name: thor-templates
description: Share a whole Thor agent as one .htemplate bundle and install it from a single HTTPS link: identity (SOUL.md), config with accounts and endpoints stripped, skills, routines, MCP server definitions, memories only when the author opts in, and plugin ids. A recipe, not a clone — credentials, sessions, conversation history, logs, caches and workspace never travel. Publish puts the bundle in a GitHub repository and returns one permanent link (re-publishing updates the same URL); Install previews a link, a path or a dropped file and shows the template itself before anything is written (SOUL.md, each skill, every routine's schedule and prompt, every MCP command, risky settings such as hooks with their values). Install enforces what the packer promises on any bundle: config sanitized again (approval and consent policy — command_allowlist, hooks_auto_accept, approvals, security — is always removed and the preview shows what was removed), routines imported paused through Thor' cron API, MCP servers set enabled: false; plugins already installed here are enabled unless --no-enable-plugins. Reinstalling the same link offers "Update v1.0.0 → v1.1.0" and keeps memories, sessions and .env. Disclosure — reads the selected profile under THOR_HOME (config.yaml, SOUL.md, skills/, cron/jobs.json, mcp.json, memories/ when opted in) and writes a new profile directory plus its own bundles under plugin-data/; the page may read a bundle only from THOR_HOME or the home directory, the CLI has no such limit. Network: one HTTPS GET to a URL the user pastes (HTTPS and public hosts only on the page; http, LAN and local accepted in the CLI; every redirect re-checked, 20 MB cap) and, only when the user presses Publish, the GitHub REST API to upload the bundle and download it back to prove the link before it is shown; republishing writes the file at the same public URL. Installs drop approval and consent policy (command_allowlist, hooks_auto_accept, approvals, security), import routines paused and turn MCP servers off; plugins already installed here are enabled unless --no-enable-plugins. Credentials: the optional GITHUB_TOKEN is read with agent.secret_scope under the named profile, never stored in a bundle, logged or returned. No shell, no telemetry, no self-updater.

name: thor-tenuo
description:
Signed, expiring tool permissions for Thor. Constrain tool names and arguments for sessions, cron jobs and delegated work, with local audit logs.
Disclosure — ordinary calls pass through until a warrant is configured. Set require_warrant: true to block calls without one. A configured but unloadable warrant blocks calls, and a kanban worker without a per-task warrant is blocked. Tool names and arguments are appended to $THOR_HOME/tenuo/audit.jsonl (disable with audit_log: false). When TENUO_CONNECT_TOKEN or TENUO_CONTROL_PLANE_URL are set, the bundled tenuo SDK (compiled Rust core) streams those decisions, including arguments, to that control plane.

name: thor-terminal
description: Run the Thor terminal interface in a Thor Desktop workspace tab.

name: thor-themes-pack
description: The 23 Omarchy stock themes (Tokyo Night, Catppuccin, Gruvbox, Nord, Rose Pine, Jade Horse and more) as Thor skins, with one /theme command that switches the CLI, the TUI and Desktop together. Optionally follows the Omarchy theme. Works without Omarchy. Disclosure — registers only the /theme command (plus a `thor theme` CLI subcommand under plugins.isolation: in_process); nothing runs at load time. /theme writes the pack's skins and a receipt under the active profile's THOR_HOME (personal or edited skins of the same name are skipped) and selects one by running `thor config set display.skin <name>`; it never edits config.yaml itself. It reads the current Omarchy theme from ~/.local/state/omarchy/current/theme.name. Only after /theme follow on does it write one executable hook into $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/omarchy/hooks/theme-set.d/; Omarchy runs it on theme switches and it switches ~/.thor and every profile under ~/.thor/profiles that has the pack installed. No network calls, background processes, Thor tools, hooks or middleware, credentials, telemetry or self-updater.

name: thor-time-machine
description: The rollback that knows what it can't undo. Incremental, time-bounded checkpoints that the agent itself can preview, restore or fork (atm_* tools, /timemachine); an approval at the point of no return (git push, npm/cargo/PyPI/gem publish, terraform apply, and MCP or plugin tools that open PRs, merge, release, send messages or deploy) that shows what becomes permanent and the exact compensation command; an effect ledger; effect memory that reminds the model of pushes it can no longer see after /rollback, /undo, /retry or compaction; and a read-only Time machine dashboard tab that shows checkpoints next to the effects no restore can undo, with per-file diffs and undo commands. Every restore takes a safety checkpoint first, so it can be undone. Disclosure — no shell commands, subprocesses, network calls, background processes or credentials; reads workspace files plus .git refs/config, package.json, Cargo.toml and pyproject.toml to capture pre-state; writes only under THOR_HOME/plugin-data/thor-time-machine, on a rewind the workspace (replaced files go to a trash directory), and on atm_fork a new sibling folder next to the workspace; adds a restore-point note to tool results and effect reminders to the model's context; asks for approval through Thor before every model-requested restore and before irreversible commands and tool calls, and never approves or blocks a tool call by itself; the dashboard tab adds three read-only GET routes (no restore, write or process); refuses filesystem roots, home and system directories.

name: thor-token-speed
description: Live decode tokens-per-second chip for the Thor Desktop status bar: 1-second sliding window while the model is still streaming, tool execution time excluded from decode seconds, UI spinner frames never counted, TTFT tracked separately, cumulative totals calibrated against authoritative provider usage at turn end. Desktop-only (desktop/plugin.js); no agent tools, hooks, middleware or env vars.

name: thor-toolsmith
description: Local developer tools, transformation recipes, and reviewed chat handoff inside Thor Desktop.

name: thor-town
description: Local pixel-art town where every Thor session is a resident and every tool call walks to a building. Passive lifecycle bridge to a loopback-only server; prompts, arguments, and output never leave the process. Disclosure — version 0.3.0 bundles the Town Node server and a prebuilt browser app inside the plugin directory and adds a thor town setup/start/status/stop/open command tree. Nothing is downloaded and no npm install runs at any point; node (^20.19 or >=22.12) must already be installed and is launched only by the explicit thor town start command, bound to 127.0.0.1 only. Runtime state, a 0600 bridge token, a bounded event journal and rotated server logs are written under THOR_HOME/thor-town/runtime/. On start the server also reads THOR_HOME/cron/jobs.json (job id and enabled flag only) to place one resident per enabled scheduled job.

name: thor-tripo
description: Tripo 3D tools on Tripo's v3 API (openapi.tripo3d.ai). Text, photo or multiview to 3D, image edits, retexturing, splitting into parts, Smart UV, auto-rigging, preset animations, retopology, format conversion (FBX, USDZ, STL, 3MF, OBJ, GLTF) and downloads, with an inline 3D viewer in Thor Desktop that shows whether a model is really rigged, a library pane that shows where each model came from (the steps behind it, its prompt, a jump back to the chat that made it, and one-click next steps), a local model inspector, and a status-bar chip with the Tripo balance and this chat's spend. Every credit-spending call goes through Thor's approval prompt with its estimated cost, and a per-chat limit (a setting under Settings → Plugins, default 100 credits) makes it ask again past it. Needs TRIPO_API_KEY. Unofficial; not affiliated with Tripo or VAST. Disclosure — sends prompts and the local images or 3D model files you or the agent name (up to 50 MB; every local-file upload, free calls included, goes through Thor's approval prompt) to Tripo's API at openapi.tripo3d.ai with TRIPO_API_KEY; saves downloaded models to $THOR_HOME/tripo/ or a folder the agent picks (never overwriting: a clash gets a " (2)" suffix), and the Desktop viewer's save button copies models into your Downloads/Tripo folder (or the folder set in its settings); keeps a local task history in $THOR_HOME/tripo/history.json (chat id, tool, prompt, parent task, estimated cost, saved file paths; at most 2,000 tasks, never sent anywhere); the Desktop library opens local .glb/.fbx/.obj/.stl files only from inside your home folder, $THOR_HOME/tripo/ or the viewer's download folder, and uploads nothing; the status-bar chip reads your Tripo balance every two minutes and after each Tripo tool call; no shell commands, background processes or telemetry.

name: thor-trove
description: DAG-based context engine that never loses a message — full-text search, semantic recall, assertion-backed evidence compilation, and pre-answer sufficiency gating Disclosure — replaces the context engine and stores every turn's full raw transcript in THOR_HOME/trove.db with secret redaction OFF by default; with TROVE_EMBEDDING_PROVIDER=voyage, transcript text is sent to Voyage AI for embeddings; as a fallback it reads private AIAgent attributes read-only via frame inspection. No other network egress.

name: thor-tube
description: Take back control of what you watch. ThorTube puts your YouTube subscriptions in Thor Desktop: tabs you make by folder, tag, channel or topic, a folder pane, a channel manager with undo, folder suggestions from your Thor model, topic tabs it builds from YouTube search, and videos in Thor's own player. New and still experimental: a cleanup list you approve, /tube buttons on Telegram and scheduled routines. Disclosure — the gateway fetches public www.youtube.com pages only (channel feeds and pages, uploads and Shorts playlists, video, /shorts and search pages, also in a background pass after refreshes), without login, and, for the favorites routine's Telegram message, one cover image per new video from i.ytimg.com; it connects to public addresses only and sends YouTube's anonymous consent cookie SOCS=CAI to YouTube hosts only; Desktop loads thumbnails and avatars from YouTube's image hosts and plays videos in Thor's own embed. A separately installed Chrome extension, the only link to the YouTube account, unsubscribes only channels a person approved in Desktop or with the /tube cleanup buttons, and talks to a plugin server on 127.0.0.1 (ports 47615-47624) paired with a 6-digit code; the approve and pairing RPCs accept any client authenticated to the gateway. Organize, cleanup reasons and topic tabs send channel names and video titles to the user's model through ctx.llm, also from unattended blueprint jobs. After a button confirmation, /tube routines writes scripts to THOR_HOME/scripts and creates cron jobs. The favorites routine sends each new video to Telegram by running thor send with a fixed argument list; it reads cron/jobs.json read-only to find the chat and never reads the bot token. Only on a click in Desktop, Set up the extension copies the extension bundled in the plugin to a fixed ThorTube Extension folder in the home folder (refusing one it did not create) and opens the Extensions page of one Chromium browser (chosen from a closed list of those found in fixed install places; no profile is read) and the file manager with fixed argument lists and time limits; a second button only drafts a fixed help request in a new chat, which the person sends. Data in THOR_HOME/plugin-data/thor-tube; no shell commands, credentials or telemetry; the README lists the known limits. Formerly MyTube, by the same author; not affiliated with YouTube, Google or Thor Labs.

name: thor-tuneup
description: Shows when compaction really fires on every profile and model route, flags settings that waste quota or break prompt caching, and fixes them only after you confirm, with a diff and a backup. Disclosure — reads every Thor profile's config.yaml (and four context-length cache files) read-only, through Thor' own loader on a temporary copy, and shows the model a redacted per-profile digest; writes a profile's config.yaml only when you type a fix and confirm it (never from cron, a group chat or an agent-launched shell), after saving a backup under that profile's backups/config; when you turn receipts on it records compaction, cache and model-use metadata (never message content) in its own plugin-data folder; imports undocumented Thor resolver modules from one adapter file (validate shows rule 9 warnings); no network calls, credentials, shell commands or background processes.

name: thor-ui
description: A bespoke chat workspace for Thor Desktop and the Webapp: it takes over the app's home route and replaces it with a three-column page — a rail of bots (one row per profile, each with its own conversations), the conversation itself with folded reasoning and tool runs, and a right panel for files, previews and session detail. Bots can answer with a structured block that the thread draws as rich components (status cards, tables, checklists, approval prompts) instead of prose; slash commands, per-bot models and a settings page come with it, and media blocks render images, audio and video inline. Disclosure — takes over the Desktop/Webapp home route by default: opening home or a session from the native sidebar redirects into Thor UI (a palette command turns this off). Its side panel previews files that replies name (MEDIA: lines, attached-image paths) by reading them through the plugin's own backend routes, which accept any path under the profile home or the user's home directory except core-refused and credential files (.env*, auth.json, config.yaml, credentials, webhook_subscriptions.json, private keys, .ssh/.aws/.gnupg, secrets, mcp-tokens and pairing folders); previews stay on the device. The bots rail reads each profile's state.db read-only, and the usage meter calls https://opencode.ai/zen/go/v1/usage only when the active profile holds OPENCODE_GO_API_KEY, with the key kept server-side. No telemetry.

name: thor-ui-cards
description: Interactive answer cards in Thor Desktop and the Webapp; your answer goes back as the next message. Disclosure — stores every Desktop card and the user's answers, free text typed into cards included, in the profile's plugin-data/thor-ui-cards/ (answers.db plus the newest 500 card files; nothing expires by time and deleting a chat does not delete its entries); adds turn context for the model (card answers, confirm-card actions and commands, and a periodic Desktop hint to use cards); Desktop cards load images from https URLs the model supplies, so the image host sees the user's IP; read-only backend routes /api/plugins/thor-ui-cards/answers and /settings; no telemetry, no credentials, no shell commands.

name: thor-unlimited
description: Create and operate AI-native provider organizations with scoped services and Thor tasks. Disclosure — Creates and reads Thor Kanban tasks (run by your Thor workers as the current profile) through the local `thor kanban` CLI on a per-tenant board, and stores company, service and request records in a local SQLite file you configure; sends your JustYou session token only to a loopback JustYou validator you configure.

name: thor-ussd
description: Use Thor from any phone, including feature phones with no internet: dial a USSD code for an instant menu, ask a question, get the agent's answer by SMS, and read long answers back page by page on USSD. Africa's Talking (Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Nigeria, Malawi and more). Closed by default (allowlist), phone users get the `safe` toolset, store-first at-most-once SMS outbox, daily SMS cap. Disclosure — opens an HTTP listener on 127.0.0.1:8790 (loopback; the user exposes it through their own tunnel or reverse proxy); makes outbound HTTPS calls only to api.africastalking.com / api.sandbox.africastalking.com (SMS API), sending reply text and the recipient's number; every question and reply crosses the mobile operator and Africa's Talking as plain-text USSD/SMS; stores phone numbers and reply text in a 0600 SQLite file in Thor plugin storage (7-day default retention, `thor ussd purge`); runs an outbox worker and an hourly purge task inside the gateway process; Africa's Talking callbacks are unsigned, so the secret URL path is the only authentication (rotate with `thor ussd rotate-secret`), and anyone holding that URL or spoofing an allowlisted sender number gets an agent turn with this profile's memory and the `safe` toolset (web, vision, image generation) by default; `AT_ALLOW_ALL_USERS=true` lets any phone start turns on the user's account; sending SMS costs money on the user's Africa's Talking account (daily cap of 200 on by default); `thor ussd setup` writes its own AT_* values to the Thor .env; no telemetry, no shell commands, no self-update, no binaries.

name: thor-vault-broker
description: Fill saved logins from an out-of-process credential broker. The broker runs as its own system user with ProtectHome=yes, derives a KEK from a passphrase with scrypt and keeps the random data key (DEK) in checked mlock'd memory, and writes the password into the page itself over a DevTools endpoint taken ONLY from its own root-owned loopback config — the model cannot choose it, and a tab's websocket is refused unless its host:port matches. The agent sends (handle, origin) over a unix socket and gets a fill count back; SO_PEERCRED limits the gateway uid to status/list/fill while unlock/add/remove/init/lock stay with root and the broker's own uid. Exact-origin binding is re-asserted inside the tab immediately before the write. Import only accepts a JSON export the operator made themselves; the broker never opens Thor's credential stores. An optional CDP-pipe mode lets the broker launch and own Chromium with no TCP debugging port. Linux; stdlib unittest suite; deps cryptography + websockets. Disclosure — requires running `scripts/install.sh` as root, which creates a `vaultd` system user, adds the Thor user to its group, pip-installs `cryptography` and `websockets` into /opt/thor-vault-broker/venv and enables a system-wide `thor-vault-broker` systemd service; saved passwords are typed into browser pages over the Chrome DevTools endpoint configured in /etc/thor-vault-broker/cdp.json, so any process running as the browser's user can read a filled field or take over that port; the optional unlock page (`unlock-form`) serves the passphrase form over self-signed HTTPS and the README suggests binding it to 0.0.0.0.

name: thor-vcc
description: Algorithmic (no-LLM) context compaction engine: builds summaries by deterministic regex extraction instead of a summarizer-model call — zero-token, byte-reproducible, inside the built-in ContextCompressor; compacted turns stay searchable via session_search. Disclosure — no network calls, no env vars, no secrets, no telemetry; registers no tools/hooks/middleware and reads only the turns the host passes for compaction; debug: true (default false) writes one metadata-only file $THOR_HOME/vcc-debug.json. Derived from pi-vcc (MIT, sting8k)

name: thor-vcc-engine
description: Instant context compaction for Thor Agent: builds the compaction summary in milliseconds with no LLM call, keeping the exact commands, exit codes, errors and files, each linked back to its original message for recall via session_search. Disclosure — no network calls, shell commands or credentials; reads Thor's config.yaml through Thor's own loader; subclasses ContextCompressor and relies on its private methods and on private helpers and constants in Thor's agent.context_compressor, conversation_compression, auxiliary_client, agent_init and skill_commands modules and thor_cli.plugins.get_plugin_commands, falling back to the stock compressor if they are missing; with the opt-in only_local_models setting, compaction for a non-local chat model goes to Thor's stock LLM summary; the /vcc chat command, available to anyone allowed to chat with the agent, switches that for hosted models for the whole profile and stores the choice in <THOR_HOME>/vcc_state.json, the only file it writes.

name: thor-verifier
description: Attach an independent verifier (advisor) model to your Thor session: it reviews each primary-agent turn delta, raises findings (note / caution / blocker), and can steer a blocker back into the session before the primary agent goes wrong. Read-only tool access (read_file, search_files) is available but off by default and best treated as opt-in plumbing -- measured across 216 reviews the reviewer made ~4 tool calls. Supports a VERIFIER.yml roster of named specialists, each with its own model and tool grant, plus VERIFIER.md review priorities. Ships disabled and off by default. Disclosure — off by default. When enabled, each primary turn's regex-redacted transcript delta goes to the verifier model's provider on that provider's terms and billing (one or more calls per turn per roster entry). So do any VERIFIER.md / VERIFIER.yml briefs found in THOR_HOME and from the working directory up to the repo root (confined to that root, 256 KiB per file). A project VERIFIER.yml can add named verifiers and instructions whose findings are injected into your session, and a blocker finding can keep a coding turn going. With advisor_tools on, an advisor can read any file the session can read through read_file/search_files, and those reads also go to the provider. The optional engagement gate sends a ≤1,500-char redacted digest per turn. The optional phase gate sends the redacted arguments of an impending destructive or publishing tool call and can block that call (it fails open). Findings, reasoning, short redacted excerpts and gate decisions are logged under THOR_HOME/plugin-data/thor-verifier (rotated at 8 MB). Adds a /verify command, a dashboard API and a Desktop Verifier page. Development scripts (evals/, sidecar/, autoresearch/) run only when launched by hand: provider experiments use DEEPSEEK_API_KEY from the process environment or the host `thor` CLI, and offline analysis reads the active profile's session database and decision logs. No telemetry, no runtime shell execution, no access to Thor's stored credentials.

name: thor-verify
description: Configurable tool-risk flags, bounded local receipt metadata and held unverified-prose labels. Disclosure — prepends an "unverified agent prose" banner to every final reply (stored in the transcript), holds streaming so replies arrive only after labeling, and replaces any reply over 100,000 characters with an omission notice; the verify_claim tool fetches model-supplied public http(s) URLs (private addresses refused); flagged tool calls are logged locally and blocked only when blocking_mode is on.

name: thor-video-editor
description: Local video editor for your own footage: 45 FFmpeg tools for the agent (cut, silence removal, 9:16 reframe, captions, music with ducking, loudness, platform export and checks) plus a visual editor in Thor Desktop with canvas, any number of tracks for text, shapes, video overlays and music, scenes and an English/German help. 100% local, no API key. Licence: PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0. Disclosure — the Desktop page starts a local web server on 127.0.0.1 (random port, per-run token) that can read and write media and image files anywhere under your home folder (and any VE_EDITOR_ROOTS); preview caches go to the system temp folder. The agent tools run ffmpeg/ffprobe on the input paths the model passes and write media, image or .srt files at the output paths it passes (replacing an existing file only with overwrite: true).

name: thor-vision-inline
description: Attach an image inline to the session model when it can see one, instead of letting an explicit auxiliary.vision backend describe it. Core already attaches images natively by default; what this plugin changes is an explicit auxiliary.vision setting, which it overrides so the model reads the pixels directly. The image stays in context, so follow-ups do not reprocess it. The model's modality comes from the local models.dev cache; no network calls and nothing to configure. Disclosure — replaces the vision_analyze handler through tool_execution middleware: when the local models.dev cache says the main model takes images and its provider carries images in tool results, it attaches the image itself even if you configured an auxiliary.vision backend (agent.image_input_mode: text still turns this off); the image stays in the conversation and is resent on later turns; relies on Thor private vision helpers, so after a Thor update it may silently fall back to the normal path.

name: thor-visual-memory
description: Your agent remembers what a camera saw on your desk: "what's in front of you?", "what did I take away?", "where did I last see my keys?", "what was here yesterday?". Built for a used Echo Show running Thor Eye, with before/after pictures on its screen. Vision goes through Thor's own model routing (its own "Visual memory" slot) or a local OpenAI-compatible model such as Qwen 3.6 in Ollama. Disclosure — off until the user turns it on by voice; the first tool call starts background threads inside Thor: a camera loop reading one snapshot a second from Thor Eye on the LAN (only while on), a token-protected API on 127.0.0.1:28950, and a LAN display feed (port 28951) restricted by client IP and the Home Assistant screen origin; pictures go to the vision model Thor routes the task to (a cloud provider if that is the user's vision model) or to the local server the user sets; SQLite and snapshots in the plugin's data directory, pictures deleted after 14 days; reads EYE_TOKEN through Thor; no shell commands, no telemetry.

name: thor-vitals-light
description: CPU, load, free RAM, Linux PSI CPU pressure, active sessions, running Thor processes and round-trip time of the connected Thor server in the Desktop status bar, plus an optional TUI card. Disclosure — the Desktop chip's backend route reads CPU/memory figures via psutil, Linux /proc/pressure/cpu and /proc/meminfo, every process's command line (only per-command Thor process counts are returned) and the server's own loopback /api/status, and reports the server hostname to the Desktop; the optional TUI card, copied by hand into tui-widgets/, runs the same code as a long-lived `python3 -c` child of the TUI and saves its options to <THOR_HOME>/vitals.json; no third-party network call, no telemetry, no credentials.

name: thor-vnc
description: Computer-use backend that drives any machine reachable over VNC (RFB): the stock computer_use tool captures the remote screen and moves that machine's mouse and keyboard, so the agent can work on a second computer, a lab box or a cloud desktop with no Thor process running on it. Select it with computer_use.backend: thor-vnc and point computer_use.vnc.host at the target. VNC carries pixels only, so the backend runs in the screenshot lane: capture returns a PNG and no accessibility elements, element-addressed actions (click-by-element, focus_app, set_value) report unsupported_action instead of guessing, and list_apps / list_windows return empty lists rather than inventing an inventory. capture_max_width downscales each capture — vision tokens scale with the image's area, so this is the one setting that changes what a screenshot costs (measured 1920 -> 786 estimated tokens at 1024 wide on a 1600x900 desktop). It also ships an optional desktop pane that shows the remote screen while the agent works — off by default, a viewer that opens its own read-only connection and never sends input. Disclosure — connects only to the VNC server you configure (host and port) and sends it screenshots and input; RFB traffic (screen pixels, keystrokes, clipboard text) is unencrypted, so use it over a private network or an SSH tunnel; the one credential is the VNC password, read from the variable named by password_env through Thor's secret scope and never written or logged; computer_use.vnc.host/port can also be overridden by the THOR_VNC_HOST / THOR_VNC_PORT / THOR_VNC_PASSWORD_ENV process environment variables; no shell, no files written, no telemetry; one daemon thread runs Twisted's reactor, started on first connect and deliberately never stopped because the reactor is process-wide and cannot be restarted; the optional desktop live-view pane (off by default) opens a second read-only VNC connection served through the plugin's dashboard route; one dependency (vncdotool>=1.2,<2).

name: thor-voice-lab
description: A voice you can play inside Thor, made by a physical model of a throat, tongue, lips and nose with air pushed through them in real time: no samples and no TTS model. Drag her tongue and lips on a side-profile portrait with a live cutaway, play notes and sing lyrics from the keyboard, beatbox on pads. The agent plays her too: it speaks lines, writes songs and beats, changes her voice, and jams with you (play a phrase, pause, and Thor sings an answer). Disclosure — local synthesis only, no network calls. Agent renders and the optional read-aloud provider run node runtime/render.mjs (the plugin's own bundled script; fixed argv, no shell, 120 s timeout) and write WAVs and projects under the plugin's data folder; Desktop export and import use only a folder the user grants. With Jam switched on, each phrase you play is sent to the focused conversation as your message. MIDI access only on request. runtime/voice_lab_engine.wasm is built from the repo's Rust source in GitHub Actions and attested; desktop/plugin.js is the esbuild bundle of src/ and inlines the same engine. Optional read-aloud provider, off unless tts.provider is set to voice-lab. No telemetry.

name: thor-vpn
description: Named network exits for the agent's browser: ask it to browse from another country and it switches, then verifies by reading back the address the far end actually saw, never trusting a label. Any VPN, WireGuard config or proxy works as a local exit; gluetun containers are discovered automatically and one can be brought up on demand. VPN credentials never reach the agent, the chat or the model. Disclosure -- a root-owned helper, installed out of band by the user through a narrow exact-path sudoers rule, is the only thing that reads the credentials and writes them to a root-only file (the agent names a country, never the key), and it pulls the gluetun image pinned by digest; the helper manages gluetun Docker containers, bringing exits up and down; the plugin registers a tool_execution middleware that holds browser_* calls when no verified exit is up (the kill switch, and optional cross-provider failover); it verifies exits by calling public IP-geolocation services (ipinfo, ifconfig.co, ip2location, cloudflare); credential entry is CLI-only, with no model tool for it -- `thor vpn provider <name> --set` (interactive) or `--from-ref`, which resolves a WireGuard config from pass/gopass or a host file host-side and never returns it to the model; opening a .onion needs `thor vpn allow-onion`, a terminal command a person runs (no model tool) that turns off Thor's own internal-address check so onion names resolve and restarts Thor, and the plugin never writes that setting itself; the active profile comes from the plugin context (ctx.profile_name), not a private core import.

name: thor-wake
description: Wakes the exact chat session (Matrix room, Telegram forum topic, ...) that started detached background work (systemd-run unit, PID or file) when that work ends, so the agent reports back on its own instead of the human asking "any updates?". Tools: wake_me_when, wake_list. Disclosure: runs the public 'thor kanban' CLI (board thor-wake, notify-subscribe --delivery-mode wake) and systemctl show; a daemon thread polls watches every 15s; stores watch targets, notes and origin ids in local SQLite under plugin-data/thor-wake; makes no network calls of its own; adds a one-line hint to terminal output of detached commands via transform_terminal_output.

name: thor-wallet
description: All of DeFi. One conversation. Thor Wallet by CoinFello makes your agent the only DeFi interface you need: swap, bridge, lend, LP, trade perps, farm yield and automate strategy from your own CoinFello wallet. Fello, CoinFello's DeFi agent, plans and stages each step, and nothing runs until you approve your agent's transaction summary in Thor, inside a daily spending limit CoinFello enforces. The wallet pane covers portfolio, activity, swap, send, earn, strategies and settings. Built by jacobc.eth, former Lead Managing Director at MetaMask. Sign-in is the plugin's oauth: entry (thor auth add coinfello:coinfello, OAuth 2.1 + PKCE against app.coinfello.com); Thor stores and refreshes the grant and the plugin never holds a token. Disclosure — crypto wallet: the agent can move funds from your CoinFello automation wallet (keys held and signing done by CoinFello's server) within the daily limit you approve on CoinFello; coinfello_execute and every coinfello_chat message go through Thor' approval prompt, and Fello can carry out on-chain actions from an approved chat message. Talks to app.coinfello.com (which records a daily activity event per session with your account id and wallet address), LI.FI's status API (li.quest), public chain RPCs (publicnode.com and others) for swap-venue lookup, static.cx.metamask.io for token icons and Google Fonts in cards; stores non-secret wallet/card state under the Thor home and the plugin directory; the open Desktop pane polls status and balances.

name: thor-wallpaper
description: Put any image, GIF or short video from your drive behind the whole Thor Desktop window. Pick it with the normal file dialog or drop it in, then tune opacity, blur, brightness, saturation, contrast, vignette, fit, anchor, zoom and mirroring; videos get speed, pause-when-hidden and reduced-motion controls, and a small library with an optional slideshow keeps several backgrounds. Quick controls in the status bar, a full settings page and command-palette commands. Disclosure — desktop-only (desktop/plugin.js, imports only @thor/plugin-sdk and react): no backend, agent tools, hooks, env vars, network calls or telemetry. Picked files are copied into the plugin's own IndexedDB in the Desktop app's local profile and never leave that computer; settings use ctx.storage. While a wallpaper shows, the plugin adds its own fixed z-index -1 layer and one style tag under its own html attribute that applies Desktop's glass-mode transparent-surface rules (surface CSS variables, [data-contrib-shell] and [data-slot='sidebar-wrapper'] fills; data-glass-opaque/raised surfaces stay filled); turning it off or disabling the plugin removes all three.

name: thor-walrus-memory
description: Append-only memory with temporal provenance and hash-chain integrity. Corrections are appended next to the original instead of overwriting it, recall returns the exact ledger line behind any fact, and with Walrus credentials every line is also stored on Walrus Mainnet. Runs zero-config as a local tamper-evident ledger with no external Python dependencies. All file access is confined to the profile: the ledger lives under plugin-data/thor-walrus-memory, and memory_import reads only the profile's own memories/MEMORY.md. It does not touch memory.provider, so it runs alongside the built-in MEMORY.md rather than replacing it. Disclosure - when WALRUS_DELEGATE_KEY and WALRUS_ACCOUNT_ID are set, every memory line (facts, corrections and derived rules) is uploaded to the Walrus Memory relay (relayer.memory.walrus.xyz by default) under the configured namespace. Lines are sent over TLS and sealed with Mysten SEAL at the relay before they are written to Walrus; the plaintext is not sealed on this machine. Offline that is the whole payload: no telemetry, no other network calls, and nothing is written to ~/.thor/MEMORY.md. Without credentials nothing leaves the machine. Reading sealed blobs back requires a SEAL session, supplied through WALRUS_SEAL_SESSION or an optional WALRUS_SEAL_BRIDGE command; nothing is pulled or decrypted without one. Disclosure — when WALRUS_DELEGATE_KEY and WALRUS_ACCOUNT_ID are set, every memory line (facts, corrections and derived rules) is uploaded to the Walrus Memory relay (relayer.memory.walrus.xyz by default, or MEMWAL_SERVER_URL) under the configured namespace; lines travel in plaintext inside TLS and are sealed with Mysten SEAL at the relay, not on this machine; reading sealed lines back runs the optional WALRUS_SEAL_BRIDGE command you configure, with a minimal environment. Without credentials nothing leaves the machine.

name: thor-web-crawl4ai
description: Self-hosted Crawl4AI extraction and bounded, policy-checked website crawling.

name: thor-webmcp-guard
description: Permission-aware, ephemeral WebMCP capabilities with origin allowlists, schema validation, conservative risk classification, exact one-call approvals, and safe revocation. Disclosure — connects only to Chrome DevTools WebSocket endpoints you configure and calls the tools the websites on your allowed origins expose; those websites may make their own network requests and their tool output reaches your model. Calls the plugin classifies as write or sensitive ask you first, but the classification uses the website's own tool names, so a site on an allowed origin can present a state-changing tool under a read-style name that runs without a prompt; allow only origins you trust. It does not launch a browser, read credentials, execute arbitrary JavaScript, or persist website capabilities.

name: thor-whatsapp-voice
description: Live voice calls with Thor over WhatsApp, on the linked-device (personal number) setup most Thor users already have, with no WhatsApp Business account. Call your bot's number and talk to your Thor: the voice uses Thor's own persona (a short briefing fetched from Thor) and hands real work to Thor mid-call. Or let Thor call you for things that matter: whatsapp_call_owner rings only the configured owner number (it has no destination parameter) and reports answered, no answer or declined, so the agent can fall back to another channel, including from cron. A short summary of each call arrives in WhatsApp, and each call keeps a record with timing metrics (thor whatsapp-voice calls). Speech runs on Gemini Live (gemini-3.8-live by default), reusing the Gemini key Thor already has; every call setting (languages, pauses, timeouts, any Live setup field) is configurable. Optional chat-session mode (context_mode: core_session, off by default) makes the call part of the owner's WhatsApp chat with Thor. Setup is a dashboard tab (pairing QR, settings, test call) or an agent runbook skill. Disclosure — runs a separate sidecar process (Rust, built on whatsapp-rust) that the user starts or installs as a systemd/launchd user service; the binary is downloaded from this repo's GitHub release, built and attested by its release workflow, and checked against checksums pinned in the repo (plus the build attestation when the gh CLI is present). The sidecar becomes an extra linked device of the bot's WhatsApp number through an unofficial protocol, stores that session in the plugin's data directory, and answers only the owner's number. During calls it streams audio to generativelanguage.googleapis.com with GOOGLE_API_KEY or GEMINI_API_KEY (read via get_secret), along with the persona briefing, the outgoing call's reason and ask_thor results as text. It calls the local api_server with API_SERVER_KEY for ask_thor (a full Thor turn with the owner's tools), the persona briefing (at startup and after each call) and the post-call summary, a run that may write to Thor memory and whose result is sent to the owner on WhatsApp. The dashboard tab's backend saves only this plugin's settings (through thor config set), starts and stops pairing, places test calls to the owner, and restarts the sidecar service (systemctl --user or launchctl). A pre_gateway_dispatch hook sends the owner's WhatsApp DM texts into an active chat-session call instead of a second text reply (slash commands, media, groups and other chats are untouched). Chat-session mode (opt-in) also runs a loopback service inside Thor's process that reads the owner's WhatsApp DM session (system prompt, recent history, tool schemas) and sends it to Gemini, runs only the tools listed in voice_tools through Thor in that session, and writes the call into that session. It never answers Thor approval prompts: a command that needs approval is denied during the call and the owner is told to ask again in the WhatsApp text chat; it imports private Thor modules (listed in the repo's CORE_PATCHES.md) and falls back to the default mode if they change. Optional recording (record_calls, off) saves the owner's side of each call as WAV in the plugin's data directory, locally only. An advanced voice_api_url setting can point the Live connection at another endpoint, which then receives the Gemini key and call audio. No telemetry.

name: thor-whoop
description: Your own WHOOP data in Thor: today's recovery, HRV, resting heart rate, SpO2, skin temperature, sleep and strain against your personal 30-day baseline, history over any date range and 7-vs-30-day trends, from the official WHOOP API v2 with your own WHOOP developer app. Adds a /whoop command that answers without a model call, two Automation Blueprints (morning readiness brief, weekly review), an opt-in readiness hook and a bundled skill. Includes a clearly labelled synthetic demo mode. Native Python plugin, no dependencies. Unofficial; not affiliated with WHOOP, Inc. Disclosure: network calls go only to api.prod.whoop.com and are made by Thor through credentialed_provider_request; the WHOOP OAuth client is declared under oauth: and signed in with `thor auth add thor-whoop:whoop`, so Thor stores and refreshes the grant and the plugin never receives a token; WHOOP_CLIENT_ID and WHOOP_CLIENT_SECRET (your own app) are optional_env read only by Thor. Health data returned by the tools enters the conversation and is sent to your model provider; /whoop in a group chat shows it to that chat. The pre_llm_call hook is off by default; when enabled it appends a one-line readiness summary to matching messages. Creates no files of its own (settings changes are written to the profile's config.yaml by Thor); WHOOP responses are cached in memory for 5 minutes. No shell commands, no background processes, no telemetry, no self-updates. Not medical advice.

name: thor-wincred
description: Resolve Thor environment variables from the current user's Windows Credential Manager at startup, instead of keeping provider keys in plaintext in .env or auth.json. Config is secrets.wincred.map, an ENV_VAR -> generic-credential-target mapping (bare names or wincred:// names); each value is read with CredReadW in the current user's vault and handed to the secret-source orchestrator, which applies it with the usual precedence, provenance and conflict rules. Values may be UTF-8 or UTF-16LE (cmdkey and the Credential UI write UTF-16); anything that does not decode to text, or that contains interior NULs, is skipped with a warning instead of being injected as a mangled key. Disclosure - this source reads your Windows Credential Manager: only the generic credentials named in the map, with no enumeration of the vault. Resolved values become environment variables of the Thor process and its children, exactly like .env entries, so anything that can read that environment can see them. The package is read-only and stdlib-only (ctypes): it never creates, updates or deletes credentials, writes no files, starts no subprocesses, makes no network calls and does not self-update. Windows only. Credential Manager is user-scoped, so this raises the at-rest bar for backups, cloud sync and dotfiles; it is not a boundary against code already running as the same user. Applying fetched values stays the orchestrator's job; the plugin never writes os.environ itself. Disclosure — when enabled, reads only the Windows Credential Manager generic credentials named in secrets.wincred.map (no vault enumeration) and injects them as environment variables of the Thor process and its children, exactly like .env entries; read-only, stdlib ctypes, no subprocesses, no network, no file writes; user-scoped at-rest protection, not a boundary against code already running as the same user.

name: thor-windows-apps
description: Answer "what is installed on this Windows machine": the software inventory behind Apps & Features, swept straight from the four Uninstall registry keys (the machine's 64-bit and 32-bit views plus the user's), so a program is found even when the Settings page hides it - a per-user install that never shows on the machine page came from the user view on the writing machine. Each row carries version, publisher, size in MB, install date and which view it lives in; the same DisplayName in two views is a 32/64-bit dual install, marked instead of listed twice. Entries the publisher asked to hide (runtime packages, update rollups) are filtered out unless asked for. Details one program with every field its publisher wrote and a reading of the uninstall command (MSI product code, setup executable, appx, script) so the next step is known before anything is run; the install folder is checked against disk. Use it for "what did that installer actually register", for inventory before a cleanup, and for "which of the two installs does uninstalling remove". Read-only: registry keys are enumerated and uninstall strings are reported, never run; no network, no file writes, no elevation. The sweep is pure registry - 102 entries in seven milliseconds on the writing machine, the whole table in ten, no PowerShell, no WMI. The plugin declares no Python dependencies. Windows only. Disclosure - the tools report program names, versions, publishers, sizes, install folders and uninstall commands, and what is hidden from Apps & Features, to the model; treat the output like the machine's own Apps & Features page.

name: thor-windows-certificates
description: Answer "which certificate on this Windows machine expired, and what am I actually trusting": walks the user's and the machine's certificate stores (MY, Root, CA) in-process through crypt32 - no certutil, no PowerShell - and lists every certificate with subject, issuer, validity window, self-signed or not, SHA-1 thumbprint and the store it lives in; the expiry arrives in words ("expired 45 days ago", "expires in 12 days") and the list is sorted with the expired and soon-expiring first. One certificate in full adds the serial number, certificate version, the signature algorithm in words, the public key's algorithm, named curve and size in bits (2048-bit RSA, P-256), and the purposes it is valid for (server authentication, code signing...; no EKU extension is reported as "does not restrict its purposes", which is what its absence means). Find it by thumbprint or by a subject substring, across the user's and the machine's copies. Use it for "why does TLS keep failing on this box", "is the root store healthy", and "which personal certificate ran out". Read-only: stores are opened read-only and only enumerated - nothing is added, removed or changed; no network, no file writes, no elevation, no child processes; 121 certificates across both contexts and all three stores walk in about 8 ms on the writing machine. Windows only. Disclosure - the tools report certificate subjects, issuers, validity windows and thumbprints, to the model; treat the output like the machine's own certificate manager page.

name: thor-windows-computer-use
description: THEIA — The Human Environment Intelligence Aperture: virtual-desktop capture, fused stage observation, guarded caches, bounded dynamic workflows, and persistent raw-RGB LocateAnything C++/Q5 CUDA grounding.

name: thor-windows-devices
description: Answer "which device on this Windows machine is unhappy, and what does it need" on Windows: win_device_table lists every present PnP device with its class (System, Net, HIDClass, Display), its status, its manufacturer, its stable device id, and its problem code in words - 28 is one with no driver installed, 10 one that cannot start, 43 one Windows stopped after it reported a failure, 22 one the person switched off on purpose and is not broken - filtering by name or id substring, by class, or to the devices that need attention; devices no longer plugged in are history, left out unless asked for. win_device_detail takes one device by id or name substring and adds the driver behind it from the signed-driver table - name, version, date, provider, signer, INF file, signed or not - or the absence of one, which for code 28 is the same fact said twice; a disabled device gets a note saying it is on purpose, not an alarm. Use it for the Device Manager yellow-mark question without opening Device Manager, for finding what an uninstalled program left behind, and for what changed after an update. Read-only: nothing is enabled, disabled, updated or reinstalled. Both answers come from CIM (Win32_PnPEntity and Win32_PnPSignedDriver, joined by device id), whose property names, enum values and ids do not change with the display language; the human-facing device names localize and are carried through as data, never parsed. The plugin declares no Python dependencies; there is no network call and no file write. Windows only. Disclosure — the tools report device names, manufacturers, device ids and driver versions to the model, and those reveal the machine's hardware inventory and what is plugged into it; treat the output like a Device Manager window opened on their machine.

name: thor-windows-disks
description: Answer "are this machine's disks healthy, and which volume is filling up" on Windows: one table of every physical disk (model, serial, SSD/HDD/SCM, bus - nvme, sata, usb -, size, the storage stack's health word, GPT or MBR, boot/system flags, partition count) and every volume (drive letter, label, file system, capacity, free space with its percentage and a verdict, fixed/removable/network/cd-rom, the disk a volume lives on, the UNC path behind a mapped drive); volumes without a drive letter (EFI, recovery) are hidden unless asked for. win_disk_detail reads one disk or volume - by drive letter, label, model, serial or disk number - with the health in words (warning, unhealthy, and "unknown", which the storage stack reports on a perfectly healthy NVMe while OperationalStatus says ok - both are shown), the partition layout decoded from its GUID type (efi system, microsoft reserved, basic data, windows recovery), each partition's size, offset and letter, the largest contiguous free extent, and a plain-word free-space verdict (under 5 percent critical, under 10 percent low). Use it for "why is the disk slow", "will this drive fail", "where did the space go". Read-only: the storage classes are queried in one PowerShell CIM session, nothing is defragmented, formatted, resized, checked or repaired; no writes, no elevation, no network calls of its own. Enum values arrive as numbers and are decoded in the plugin - a Chinese-language Windows 11 was verified never to reach the answer; the whole table answers in about two thirds of a second. The plugin declares no Python dependencies. Windows only. Disclosure - the tools report disk models, serial numbers, sizes, health words, partition layouts, volume labels, capacities and free space, and the UNC paths behind mapped drives, to the model; treat the output like the machine's own Disk Management page.

name: thor-windows-eventlog
description: Answer "why did this process die" on Windows: three read-only tools over the Windows Event Log. win_crash_events reads Application Error / Application Hang / Windows Error Reporting / .NET Runtime records for a time window, decodes the exception code (0xC0000005 -> ACCESS_VIOLATION and the other codes a debugger would name), reports the faulting module, its path and the fault offset, and groups repeated crashes by app and signature. Records are classified by provider as well as by event id, so unrelated providers that reuse ids 1000 and 1001 for informational events are not reported as crashes. win_shutdown_events reads the System log for Kernel-Power 41 unexpected restarts, bugchecks decoded to names (0x9F -> DRIVER_POWER_STATE_FAILURE, accepting the decimal form some providers emit), EventLog 6008 dirty shutdowns, 1074 operator-initiated restarts with the process and comment, and the 6005/6006/12/13 start and stop markers. win_eventlog_query is the general case: any channel, filtered by event ids, levels, an exact provider name or a payload substring, returning structured records instead of raw XML. Queries read newest-first and stop at the window start or at a 5000-record scan cap; a call returns at most 200 records and marks truncated payload text. Channel names, provider names and numeric filters are validated before anything is interpolated into the query. Disclosure - this plugin reads the local Windows event logs and hands what it finds to the model: application and faulting-module paths, exception codes and offsets, report ids, service names and provider message text, which routinely includes user and machine paths (C:\Users\<name>\...). Treat tool output like any other local diagnostic dump when sharing it. It reads only the channels the current account may read - Security and some operational logs answer with an access-denied error rather than any attempt to obtain elevation - and it never writes to a log, clears one or configures a channel. Stdlib-only (ctypes wevtapi plus xml.etree): no Python dependencies, no child processes, no network calls, no file writes, no self-update. Windows only. Disclosure — reads the local Windows event logs and hands what it finds to the model: application and faulting-module paths, exception codes and offsets, report ids, service names and provider message text, which routinely include user and machine paths (C:\Users\<name>\...); win_eventlog_query reads any channel the account running Thor may read, so an unelevated account gets access-denied on Security and some operational logs while an elevated Thor can return Security-log records (logon events with account names and source addresses). It never requests elevation, never writes to, clears or configures a log, and has no Python dependencies, child processes, network calls, file writes or self-update. Windows only.

name: thor-windows-firewall
description: Answer "what does the Windows firewall let through, and for whom" on Windows: every rule from the registry store the firewall service itself keeps, each row in plain words -- allow or block, inbound or outbound, TCP/UDP/ICMP or a protocol number, local and remote ports, the program or service the rule is scoped to, which profile it belongs to (Domain, Private, Public or any) and whether it is switched on -- plus the three profiles' firewall switches and default actions, with values the registry did not write reported as null and attributed to Windows' builtin defaults rather than invented. Built-in rules name themselves indirectly (@FirewallAPI.dll,-32765); the words are resolved from the resource in the machine's own language, and references that will not resolve stay as written. Details one rule in full: addresses with scope words (the local subnet, any address), edge traversal, the embedding group, the description, and fields the parser does not model (TTK2_22 is on real machines) passed through verbatim rather than dropped. netsh labels localize with the display language, the registry does not -- which is why the plugin goes there: no netsh, no PowerShell, no WMI. Use it for "is port X open", "what may this exe do", and "is the firewall actually on". Read-only: registry values are enumerated and resource strings resolved, nothing is enabled, disabled, added or removed; no network calls of its own, no file writes, no elevation. The whole store answers in hundredths of a second (795 rules in 0.07 s on the writing machine); the plugin declares no Python dependencies. Windows only. Disclosure - the tools report every rule's action, direction, protocol, ports, addresses, program, service and name, and the profile switches, to the model; treat the output like the firewall page of Windows Security.

name: thor-windows-network
description: Answer "is this machine's network healthy, and which adapter is the problem" on Windows: lists every visible network adapter with its state (up, disconnected, disabled, not present), its link speed as a number, its MAC, whether it is virtual (Hyper-V, VPN, virtual switch) or physical, and its driver version and date; adapters that are only a ghost of an old dock or USB device are hidden unless asked for. Details one adapter's IPv4/IPv6 addresses with prefixes and origins (DHCP, manual, self-assigned 169.254.x.x), default gateways, DNS servers, and a plain-word diagnosis - link-local means DHCP never answered, an address without a gateway cannot leave its subnet, no DNS means names will not resolve; a disconnected adapter with a stale static DNS says all three on the writing machine. Use it for "why is there no internet", for "which of these adapters is actually in use", and for reading what DHCP left on an interface. Read-only: the NetAdapter and NetTCPIP cmdlets are queried, nothing is enabled, renewed, reconfigured or released; no network calls of its own, no file writes, no elevation. Adapter names are localized data and are passed through as-is; states travel as enum names, which a Chinese-language Windows 11 was verified not to translate. The whole table answers in under a second and one adapter's detail in about two and a half, each a single PowerShell session; the plugin declares no Python dependencies. Windows only. Disclosure - the tools report adapter names and descriptions, addresses, MACs, gateways, DNS servers and driver versions, to the model; treat the output like the machine's own adapter settings page.

name: thor-windows-ops
description: Windows and WSL triage skills for Thor: processes that survive a quit (orphaned stdio MCP trees, lingering python/uv/node children), WSL-to-Windows interop where an argument reaches cmd.exe as shell syntax, config and encoding traps (UTF-8 BOM, legacy console code pages), and long-path or reserved-name errors. One skill plus a copy-paste command reference; the process, argv and job-object failure modes are pinned to reports #131561, #132069 and #61059 and re-verified against current main. Disclosure — instructions only: no tools, hooks, middleware, network calls or credentials, and the destructive diagnostics are marked and gated on asking the user first.

name: thor-windows-ports
description: Answer "who holds this port" on Windows. win_port_owners reads the TCP and UDP owner tables through iphlpapi (the same rows netstat -ano prints, with the owning PID attached) and resolves each PID to its image name and path, returning one structured record per endpoint. Filters cover one port, several ports, a process substring, the protocol (tcp, udp or both), the TCP state (listen, established, any state name, or all; UDP rows report bound) and IPv6 inclusion, with a record cap and a per-process summary of the rows returned. Built for the failure mode that stalls agents on Windows: a gateway, backend or bridge that cannot bind, where the error names a port but not the process holding it. netstat -ano prints columns, not fields, and its PID still needs a second command (tasklist, or a PowerShell round-trip) to become an image name; this tool is one in-process call instead of a shell parse plus a join, with no child process and no dependency on PowerShell being installed or allowed by execution policy. A protected process whose image cannot be queried keeps its PID and reports a null process name instead of failing the call. Disclosure - the tool reports the local and remote addresses, ports, PIDs and process image paths that netstat -ano and Task Manager already show, and those values reach the model; treat the output like any other local diagnostic listing. Read-only: no socket is opened, bound or connected, the only process access is QueryFullProcessImageName with PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION to read an image name, and there is no memory reading, no handle inheritance and no injection. Stdlib-only (ctypes): no Python dependencies, no child processes, no network calls, no file writes, no self-update. Windows only.

name: thor-windows-process
description: Answer "what is still running, and who started it" on Windows: win_process_table reads the process table (PID, parent PID, image name) and adds each process's image path and creation time, then marks every row with whether its recorded parent is still the process that spawned it. Windows stores a parent PID rather than a handle, so a child that outlived its parent points at a PID that is either unused or reused by a newer process; a parent that started after its child cannot have spawned it, so both cases are reported as gone or reused instead of a plausible but wrong parent name. Filters cover one PID, several PIDs, a name or path substring, a parent PID, and an orphans-only view of what outlived its parent, with a result cap and an option to leave out Windows session processes. Use it for leftover gateway/backend/server children after a quit, for telling thirty python.exe rows apart by start time, and for checking whether a process started before or after the thing being debugged. Read-only: processes are opened with PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION for QueryFullProcessImageName and GetProcessTimes only - no memory reads (command lines are deliberately out of scope), no handle duplication, no writes, no child processes. Stdlib-only (ctypes): no Python dependencies, no network calls, no file writes, no self-update. Windows only. Disclosure - the tool reports image names, image paths and start times to the model, and those routinely include the user and machine name (C:\Users\<name>\...) and reveal which editor, shell or agent started which process; treat the output like a Task Manager screenshot.

name: thor-windows-services
description: Answer "what runs as a service on this machine, why did one fail, and what does it depend on" on Windows: win_service_table lists every service with its state (Running, Stopped, Paused), its start mode (Auto, Manual, Disabled, with the delayed flag folded in as "Auto, delayed"), the pid it runs under, the account and binary it runs as, the dependency edges both ways, and what its exit code means - 1077 is one that has not tried to start since the last boot, 1053 one that did not answer in time, 1075 one whose dependency failed first, 2 one whose binary is gone. win_service_detail takes one service and gives what Windows does when it fails (the FailureActions blob decoded: restart the service, restart the computer, run a command, after how many seconds, and when the count resets), whether the registered binary is still on disk, and the Service Control Manager's own event-log record behind the failure - 7000 failed to start, 7009 a start request that timed out, 7024 a service-specific error, 7031 an unexpected end, 7045 an install. Use it for what died after the last update, for finding what an uninstalled program left registered, and for the dependency order before a restart. Read-only: nothing is started, stopped, reconfigured or deleted. The listing comes from one Get-CimInstance Win32_Service call because its property names and enum values do not change with the display language while sc.exe localizes both; dependencies and failure actions are read from the registry, because CIM's DependOnService property is never populated and the failure policy exists nowhere in CIM at all. The plugin declares no Python dependencies; there is no network call and no file write. Windows only. Disclosure - the tools report service names, display names, command lines, logon accounts and the event-log history to the model, and those reveal what the person has installed, what runs as their machine's system accounts, and the paths under C:\Program Files and C:\Users\<name>; treat the output like a Services window opened on their machine.

name: thor-windows-startup
description: Answer "what launches itself on this machine" on Windows: win_startup_table lists every autostart entry across the six Run/RunOnce registry keys (HKCU and HKLM, plus the 32-bit views) and the two Startup folders, with where each one comes from, whether it is machine- or user-scoped, and whether the person switched it off in Task Manager - Explorer's StartupApproved verdict, with the date it was last changed, a state Win32_StartupCommand has no field for; approval records uninstalled programs left behind are reported as leftovers, their unknown state bytes surfaced as-is rather than guessed into verdicts. win_startup_detail takes one entry and resolves its command the way the loader does - quoting, arguments, environment variables, and unquoted paths with spaces resolved by longest existing prefix - and says whether the binary is still on disk, plus a folder file's size and last change. Use it for what added itself since last month, for slimming a slow sign-in, and for a launcher whose program is already gone. Read-only: nothing is enabled, disabled or deleted; the Startup folders are read through Explorer's User Shell Folders values so OneDrive-redirected folders are found. The sweep is registry and directory reads only - about a millisecond for three Run values and two folders on the machine it was written on, no PowerShell, no WMI. The plugin declares no Python dependencies; there is no network call and no file write. Windows only. Disclosure - the tools report program names, launch commands, binary paths under C:\Program Files and C:\Users\<name>, and what the person chose to keep from starting, to the model; treat the output like the Startup tab of the person's own Task Manager.

name: thor-windows-tasks
description: Answer "what does this machine run on its own, and did it work" on Windows: win_scheduled_tasks lists the Task Scheduler's tasks with their state (Ready, Running, Disabled), the account each runs as, its first action's command line, its triggers in words (at logon, daily, weekly, at a time, on event), its last and next run with the machine's offset, its missed runs, and what its last result code means - 0x80070002 is a program that is no longer there, 0x800710E0 a task that needed a desktop it did not have, 0x40010004 one that was stopped, 0x80040154 a COM class that is not registered. win_scheduled_task_detail takes one task and gives its triggers with start boundaries and repetition, its actions with arguments and working directory, its principal and the settings that decide whether it runs on battery or when late; a task with no triggers but MaintenanceSettings runs during automatic maintenance and the notes say so rather than leaving an empty list. Use it for why a logon task keeps failing, for finding what an uninstalled program left behind at logon, for telling a disabled task from a broken one, and for reading a task's command line before trusting it. Read-only: nothing is created, started, changed or deleted. Reads through the ScheduledTasks cmdlets rather than the store on disk, because the TaskCache registry tree and C:\Windows\System32\Tasks both answer access denied without elevation, and rather than schtasks /Query /FO CSV, which is localized and interleaves error lines for tasks whose definitions are gone. The plugin declares no Python dependencies; there is no network call and no file write. Windows only. Disclosure - the tools report task paths, command lines, working directories, account names and SIDs to the model, and those reveal what the person has installed, what starts at their logon, and the paths under C:\Users\<name>; treat the output like a Task Scheduler window opened on their machine.

name: thor-windows-updates
description: Answer "what did Windows install lately, and did it work" on Windows: the update history the Settings app shows - Windows updates, Defender signature and platform updates, driver updates - newest first, with each entry's outcome in words (in progress, succeeded, succeeded with errors, failed, aborted) and, when an entry did not end clean, the failure's error code in 0x form (the agent hands codes over signed; -2145124300 is shown as its unsigned spelling). Filter to the ones that did not end clean, or search titles. The hotfix list (KB numbers, security updates, install dates, newest first) answers "when was this machine last patched" at a glance; it carries OS-level updates only, which the notes say. Use it for "why does it say pending forever", for "did the update that broke something actually install", and for a patch report before assuming a machine is current. Read-only: the history is queried through the Windows Update Agent's session interface and CIM, and nothing else - no update search is run, nothing is downloaded, installed or uninstalled, no elevation. On the writing machine a 723-entry history returns the newest 500 in about a tenth of a second; the first call also starts the COM session, about a quarter of a second. The plugin declares no Python dependencies; there is no network call of its own and no file write. Windows only. Disclosure — each tool call runs one hidden powershell.exe with a fixed read-only script (Windows Update Agent history through COM, Win32_QuickFixEngineering through CIM; no update search, download or install); the tools report update titles, dates, outcomes, failure codes and support links, and hotfix ids, descriptions, install dates and the account that installed them, to the model; treat the output like the Settings app's own update history page.

name: thor-witness
description: Evidence-gated learning for Thor Agent. Grades each agent-written skill against the session's real tool results, tracks outcomes in later use, and quarantines grade-D skills. Deterministic and local, no LLM calls. Disclosure — reads MEMORY.md, USER.md and skills under your Thor home and grades every skill the agent creates or edits (including ones you wrote); in the default `gate` mode it moves grade-D skills to `~/.thor/witness/quarantine` (reversible with `thor witness release`); writes a local hash-chained ledger and a trace of tool names and argument keys only; no network calls, credentials, shell commands, background processes or telemetry. No dependencies, no self-updating code, no core overrides, no binaries. Release and trust are CLI-only.

name: thor-workbench
description: The Thor desktop app in your browser. `thor workbench` serves the desktop interface through the Thor dashboard, for headless servers, VPSes and tablets. Disclosure — community plugin, not a Nous product. On the first `thor workbench` run and again after each Thor update it runs `npm install --ignore-scripts` (guided by Thor's lockfile) and Vite against your Thor checkout's desktop sources, writing only under ~/.thor/thor-workbench and its own plugin dir (the checkout is only read), and starts `thor dashboard` on loopback when none is running.

name: thor-worker-monitor
description: Kanban board groups and worker health in the Thor Desktop footer: blocked cards first and red, live running state as a coloured dot, hover for the breakdown, one click to open the board. Worker-only fork of thor-monitor. No credentials are read and there is no network egress; it opens kanban.db and each profile's state.db read-only and returns counts only. Zero model tokens.

name: thor-workflows
description: Agent-owned workflow graphs for Thor — a background runner executes a JSON DAG of agent nodes, fan-outs (quorum) and human/machine gates with fingerprint replay-skip resume, cooperative steer, typed failure events and compact status payloads; ships a desktop DAG view, an inline transcript card and the authoring skill with measured budget recipes. Stock Thor; no patched core required. Disclosure — every workflow run spawns a detached background runner (wf.py run <id>) that survives session end, gateway restart and plugin disable until the graph reaches a boundary or workflow stop; each agent node is a child thor chat --query-file … --oneshot -Q … inheriting the runner's environment, and a node with profile set runs as that named profile (with its own credentials) only if the target's workflow_team.json lists the launcher; a gate's wait.until_argv and a fan-out's precheck_argv (run once per item before its child spawns) run agent-authored argv directly from the runner, outside Thor' tool-approval gate (the engine uses no shell, but the shipped machine-watch and incident-response templates use until_argv to run a shell line read from a fixed-name handoff file under $THOR_HOME, and release-lifecycle one read from a per-run handoff file in the run dir); the runner makes itself the subreaper of its children and SIGTERM/SIGKILLs any process a node leaves running (its own descendants plus pids registered in the run's .proctree_sidecar.jsonl) when the node finishes, retries or the run stops; run and amend send a one-token ping through Thor' configured providers to check pinned model routes; at gate.held/run.done/run.failed/run.partial and fan-out straggler events the runner reads the API server key from config.yaml (or API_SERVER_KEY) and POSTs a wake turn to the configured Thor API server — the gate.held, run.done, run.failed and run.partial wakes state they authorize no choice, repair or additional work, while the straggler wake asks the woken session to take one action (steer the open items, accept the partial, or stop the run); a transform_llm_output hook appends a ::workflow{id} card line to replies for runs the session launched in the last 30 minutes; the runner reads WORKFLOW_MAX_SEATS (that key only) from $THOR_HOME/.env and the active profile's .env; state.db is read read-only, including every profile's session ids and profile names, and status/wait can read runs in sibling profiles' workflows dirs; opt-in settings (all default off) mirror run lifecycle events to an operator-configured https webhook with an optional bearer (outbound_bridge), present held gates into the run owner's own gateway session via plugin message injection (hooks_bridge_allow: approval_bridge, which also needs allow_gateway_injection), and append delegate_task child records to a spool under $THOR_HOME/plugin-state (hooks_allow: subagent_accounting); every accepted launch also writes an executable shim at $THOR_HOME/scripts/thor-workflows-tick.sh and arms a single thor-workflows-tick Thor cron job (no_agent, so it wakes no agent; every 2m by default, tunable via WF_TICK_SCHEDULE or workflows.tick_schedule) that revives dead runners and deletes itself once no run is active — disabling or uninstalling the plugin mid-run does not remove the job or shim; state lives under $THOR_HOME/workflows/ (or a configured runs_root). No other network of its own.

name: thor-wrapped
description: Your week with Thor as a 30-second video, delivered every Sunday: what your agent did, what it cost, and how much of your time went into upkeep versus Thor working for you. Built from Thor's own session records by code: no model calls, no tokens, secrets and home paths stripped.
